questions.question_text: Rashmi works as a reservation executive at a travel and tourism company. Though her job only requires her to efficiently book flight tickets for customers, she has also opted to undergo training in hotel reservations. In addition, every evening she reads travelogues to stay up to date on upcoming travel destinations and trends. She loves the industry she works in and is eager to learn as much as she can. Considering the information given in this case, which dimension of the Big Five model best describes Rashmi's personality?

options.A: Extroversion
options.B: Agreeableness
options.C: Conscientiousness
options.D: Openness to experience

questions.explanation: Rashmi's eagerness to learn, seek training beyond her basic role, and read travelogues reflects high curiosity and a desire for novelty, which are classic characteristics of the 'Openness to experience' dimension of the Big Five model.

questions.question_text: Extremely attractive or unattractive individuals are most likely to be noticed in a group. Which of the following statements best describes the reason behind this?

options.A: Our perception of reality depends on our past experiences.
options.B: Our perception of reality depends on our personality.
options.C: We don't look at targets in isolation.
options.D: The time at which we see an object can influence our perception of the object.

questions.explanation: Our perception of a target is heavily influenced by its relationship to its background and surrounding context. Since we do not observe targets in isolation, extreme contrast—such as high attractiveness or unattractiveness—makes individuals stand out relative to the rest of the group.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is true about people with positive core self-evaluations?

options.A: They are committed to their goals and set ambitious goals.
options.B: They view themselves as powerless over their environment.
options.C: They tend to question their capabilities and capacities.
options.D: They tend to be disliked by superiors and co-workers.

questions.explanation: People with positive core self-evaluations (CSE) view themselves as capable, effective, and in control of their environment. Consequently, they tend to set challenging, ambitious goals and maintain high commitment to achieving them.

questions.question_text: Those with a _________ personality identify opportunities, show initiative, and persevere until meaningful change occurs, compared to those with _________ which hurts job search.

options.A: high self-monitoring and low self-efficacy
options.B: proactive and low self-efficacy
options.C: high Mach and high self-efficacy
options.D: narcissist and introversion

questions.explanation: A proactive personality drives individuals to take initiative and persevere to make changes, while low self-efficacy represents a low belief in one's capability, which can discourage active and successful job searching.

questions.question_text:
Are the statements True or False?

Statement 1: The tendency to draw a general impression about an individual on the basis of a single characteristic is known as the contrast effect.

Statement 2: Stereotyping helps individuals make quick decisions through generalisations.

options.A: True and True
options.B: True and False
options.C: False and True
options.D: False and False

questions.explanation: Statement 1 is false because drawing a general impression from a single characteristic is the Halo or Horn effect, not the contrast effect. Statement 2 is true because stereotyping serves as a cognitive shortcut (heuristic) to process complex information rapidly through generalization.

questions.question_text:
Analyse the context and answer the following question

360.org, an organisation working to curb climate change, recently conducted an interview with Anirudh for the position of public relations officer. However, interviewers Ahmed and Laura disagree on whether Anirudh should be given the job. Ahmed believes that Anirudh lacks in-depth knowledge of global warming and its impact. On the other hand, Laura feels that Anirudh would be perfect for the job because he has strong networking and interpersonal skills.

Which of the following, if true, would strengthen Laura's argument?

options.A: Gaining the support of corporate giants would comprise a large part of the job.
options.B: Anirudh will need to prepare extensive reports about the issue of climate change.
options.C: The role will require Anirudh to give presentations to environmental experts on renewable modes of energy.
options.D: Anirudh had negligible experience in research and development.

questions.explanation: If the primary responsibility of the role is to secure partnerships with corporate sponsors, then strong networking and interpersonal skills are crucial requirements, thereby validating and strengthening Laura's selection criteria.

questions.question_text:
Analyse the context and answer the following question

360.org, an organisation working to curb climate change, recently conducted an interview with Anirudh for the position of public relations officer. However, interviewers Ahmed and Laura disagree on whether Anirudh should be given the job. Ahmed believes that Anirudh lacks in-depth knowledge of global warming and its impact. On the other hand, Laura feels that Anirudh would be perfect for the job because he has strong networking and interpersonal skills.

Which of the following, if true, would weaken Laura's argument?

options.A: Anirudh was unable to fare well in the written test which analyzed her conceptual skills.
options.B: Anirudh listened intently to the interviewers' questions before answering them.
options.C: Anirudh was unable to communicate clearly why she was right for the job.
options.D: Anirudh was high in confidence about getting the job because of her strong networking skills.

questions.explanation: If Anirudh cannot clearly articulate why he is the right fit during the interview, it indicates a direct failure in his core communication and interpersonal execution, which severely undermines Laura's claim that his strong interpersonal skills make him perfect for the job.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is true regarding surface acting?

options.A: It involves foregoing emotional expressions in response to display rules.
options.B: It involves changing one's likes and dislikes to be in sync with display rules.
options.C: It involves displaying one's true feelings explicitly toward a person.
options.D: It deals with expressing felt emotions toward a person or event.

questions.explanation: Surface acting involves suppressing and hiding inner, genuine emotional feelings to display required, superficial expressions in compliance with organizational emotional display rules.

questions.question_text:
Match the Following:

| Description | Concepts |
| :--- | :--- |
| P. Dheer can monitor his actions and appearance in social situations | A. Locus of control |
| Q. Rani has overall positive feelings about herself | B. Self-monitoring |
| R. Jhanvi believes that she can perform a specific task successfully | C. Self-esteem |
| S. Jay feels accountable for his behaviours | D. Self-efficacy |

options.A: P-A, Q-C, R-D, S-B
options.B: P-B, Q-C, R-D, S-A
options.C: P-D, Q-B, R-C, S-A
options.D: P-C, Q-A, R-B, S-D

questions.explanation: The matching correctly links definitions: Self-monitoring (P-B) is adapting to social situations; Self-esteem (Q-C) is positive self-regard; Self-efficacy (R-D) is task-specific confidence; and Locus of control (S-A) deals with feelings of personal accountability.

questions.question_text: Suppose a manager uses Herzberg’s theory and finds that employees are neither fully dissatisfied nor fully satisfied. Which scenario best aligns with Herzberg’s model?

options.A: Hygiene factors are at an acceptable level, but motivators are absent → employees will be in a state of “no dissatisfaction, but low satisfaction”.
options.B: Motivators are well provided, but hygiene factors are poor → employees will be in a state of “high satisfaction despite significant complaints”.
options.C: Both hygiene and motivator factors are high → employees have moderate satisfaction but also moderate complaints.
options.D: Hygiene factors are poor, and motivators are absent → employees have high satisfaction but high complaints.

questions.explanation: In Herzberg's framework, hygiene factors (such as salary and work conditions) only remove dissatisfaction, whereas motivators (achievement, recognition) actively drive satisfaction. Under this scenario, neutral hygiene factors leave employees without complaints, but absent motivators leave them unsatisfied.

questions.question_text: A manager uses both Herzberg's theory and Goal-Setting theory. Which actions would align with both? (Select all that apply)

options.A: Providing challenging objectives with clear targets
options.B: Ensuring adequate salary while setting specific performance goals
options.C: Offering recognition when goals are achieved
options.D: Ignoring working conditions to focus only on goal achievement

questions.explanation: Providing challenging objectives and clear targets serves as motivators (Herzberg) and performance drivers (Goal-Setting). Salary serves as a necessary hygiene factor, while recognition acts as a potent motivator, making A, B, and C aligned with both models.

questions.question_text: Which of the following options best explains situations where an employee perceives inequity despite high effort? (Select all that apply)

options.A: The employee believes that their outcomes are disproportionately low compared to their inputs, leading to feelings of under-reward.
options.B: The employee perceives that their inputs are greater than their outcomes, but attributes this to external market conditions rather than internal unfairness.
options.C: The employee compares their inputs and outcomes with a peer who is perceived to have similar effort but different results, leading to a perception of inequity.
options.D: The employee attributes any inequity to poor supervisor communication rather than to actual disparities in input or outcome.

questions.explanation: Equity theory states that workers evaluate equity by comparing their input/outcome ratio with referent others. Inequity is perceived when they feel under-rewarded for their inputs (A) or when they notice colleagues receiving better returns for equivalent levels of effort (C).

questions.question_text: Beyond redesigning the nature of the work itself and involving employees in decisions, another approach to making the work environment more motivating is to alter work arrangements to meet employee needs. Which of the following is designed to give employees greater control of their schedule? (Select all that apply)

options.A: Flextime
options.B: Employee Recognition programs
options.C: Compressed work week
options.D: Job Enlargement

questions.explanation: Flextime and compressed workweeks are flexible structural work design arrangements that explicitly allow employees autonomy over when and how they distribute their daily and weekly scheduled working hours.

questions.question_text: A tech company operates in a dynamic and complex environment. According to the contingency theories, which structural traits will help them survive? (Select all that apply)

options.A: High levels of decentralisation.
options.B: Low formalisation.
options.C: Strict departmentalisation.
options.D: Wide spans of control to encourage autonomy.

questions.explanation: Dynamic and volatile environments require organic organizational systems. High decentralization, low formalization, and wide spans of control minimize bureaucracy and empower rapid, locally sensitive decision-making, which is critical for tech sector survival.

questions.question_text: A global retail chain is facing a crisis because local store managers cannot react quickly to regional competitor pricing. The CEO is considering decentralising the organisation. Which of the following justifies this move? (Select all that apply)

options.A: It empowers lower-level managers to provide more detailed input.
options.B: It ensures that everyone strictly follows the "big picture" strategy.
options.C: It allows for faster tactical responses to localised problems.
options.D: It reduces the feeling of alienation among frontline employees.

questions.explanation: Decentralization yields advantages by leveraging ground-level insights (A), enabling instantaneous local execution in response to localized challenges (C), and boosting structural engagement among frontline managers by giving them authority (D).

questions.question_text: A CEO wants to ensure the company's "Spirit of Service" culture survives after she retires. Which practices help sustain a culture? (Select all that apply)

options.A: Selection processes that identify and hire people with matching values.
options.B: Top management behaving in ways that reinforce the values.
options.C: Socialisation programs to help new employees adapt.
options.D: Ignoring the "fit" to ensure a variety of opinions.

questions.explanation: Sustaining culture depends on a tripartite framework: hiring for organizational fit and value alignment during selection (A), executive modeling of the desired values (B), and systematic socialization of new employees to transition them into the corporate fold (C).

questions.question_text: A pharmaceutical company wants to become more innovative. What structural and cultural variables should they foster? (Select all that apply)

options.A: High tolerance for risk and conflict.
options.B: Low vertical differentiation (flat structure).
options.C: High formalisation and strict rules.
options.D: Focus on ends rather than means.

questions.explanation: Innovation is nurtured by organic processes. This is facilitated by a high tolerance for risk and constructive task debate, flat structures (low vertical differentiation), and evaluating employees on creative output (ends) rather than bureaucratic compliance (means).

questions.question_text: A new employee is told by the CEO to "be creative”, but is told by their direct manager to "follow the manual exactly." This employee is experiencing: (Select all that apply)

options.A: Role Ambiguity.
options.B: Role Conflict.
options.C: Role Overload.
options.D: Inter-role Conflict.

questions.explanation: The conflict of instructions between creative leeway (CEO) and strict rule adherence (manager) directly causes role conflict (incompatible expectations within the job) and role ambiguity (confusion regarding which protocol to prioritize).

questions.question_text: A retail chain is facing scandals regarding predatory sales tactics. To create a more ethical culture, management should: (Select all that apply)

options.A: Be a visible role model for ethical behaviour.
options.B: Provide ethical training and workshops.
options.C: Reward employees for achieving results, regardless of the methods used.
options.D: Visibly punish unethical acts.

questions.explanation: Developing an ethical organizational culture requires leadership modeling (A), providing clear educational guidelines on ethics (B), and enforcing visible disciplinary actions against ethical infractions (D). Rewarding results regardless of methodology (C) would only encourage predatory tactics.

questions.question_text: A team of veteran aerospace engineers is working on a high-stakes, ambiguous project. They are highly motivated, possess advanced degrees, and prefer to work without constant supervision. Which leadership actions would be redundant or diminish performance? (Select all that apply)

options.A: Providing specific, step-by-step instructions on how to perform tasks.
options.B: Setting challenging goals and expressing confidence in the team's ability.
options.C: Spending significant time providing emotional support and "cheerleading" for routine tasks.
options.D: Involving the engineers in the decision-making process regarding technical hurdles.

questions.explanation: For highly skilled, self-directed experts, directive instructions (A) are patronizing and redundant. Over-cheerleading or hand-holding on routine elements (C) is also unnecessary and can demotivate autonomous high performers.

questions.question_text: Krish discovers that the company accidentally overcharged a client. Even though the client didn't notice, he reports the error, issues a refund, and explains the lapse to the entire staff. Which leadership qualities are being demonstrated? (Select all that apply)

options.A: Acting in alignment with personal values even when it is costly.
options.B: Using "position power" to force compliance from the accounting team.
options.C: Building trust through the honest sharing of information.
options.D: Focusing on the long-term ethical health of the organisation over short-term profit.

questions.explanation: Krish's transparency demonstrates high integrity and value-driven leadership (A), which actively fosters organizational trust (C) and protects the company's long-term ethical capital and reputation over temporary profit margins (D).

questions.question_text: A department head, Sarah, has been granted the authority to hire and fire, and she is also widely respected for her 20 years of niche-industry experience and her approachable, mentoring nature. Which of the following statements regarding her power bases are correct? (Select all that apply)

options.A: Her Personal power bases (Expert/Referent) are likely to be more effective for long-term employee commitment than her Formal power.
options.B: If Sarah is promoted to a different department where her niche experience is irrelevant, she will immediately lose her Referent power.
options.C: Legitimate power is often the most unstable because it relies entirely on the person’s position in the organisational hierarchy.
options.D: Coercive power is a formal base that is most likely to result in employee resistance rather than compliance or commitment.

questions.explanation: Personal power bases generate deep commitment, whereas formal bases like legitimate and coercive powers are vulnerable to hierarchical shifts (C) and are highly prone to triggering workforce resistance rather than loyalty (D). Referent power is personal and does not vanish immediately upon transfer (making B incorrect).

questions.question_text: A software development team is constantly arguing about which programming language is most efficient for a new project. While these debates are heated and time-consuming, the team eventually produces a more robust, bug-free code than teams that agree immediately. Which of the following statements about this situation are true? (Select all that apply)

options.A: This is an example of functional conflict because it improves the quality of decisions.
options.B: The disagreements represent "Process Conflict," as they focus on the delegation of duties.
options.C: The team is experiencing "Task Conflict," which is often beneficial in non-routine activities.
options.D: Because the debates are time-consuming, the conflict is inherently dysfunctional regardless of the output.

questions.explanation: The debate is over the content of the work, which constitutes task conflict (C). Since this process results in a higher quality, more robust end product, the conflict functions constructively and is deemed functional conflict (A).

questions.question_text: Two department heads, Abhoy and Jordan, have disliked each other for years. During a budget allocation meeting, Abhoy dismisses Jordan’s proposal not because of the data, but because he finds Jordan "arrogant." Jordan reacts by becoming defensive and refusing to share resources. Which of the following are occurring? (Select all that apply)

options.A: The conflict has shifted from the "Task" level to the "Relationship" level.
options.B: This is a "Perceived Conflict," where the parties are aware of the disagreement but haven't felt the emotional impact yet.
options.C: The conflict is likely becoming dysfunctional because it is centred on personalities.
options.D: The focus has moved to "Cognition and Personalisation," where emotions start to influence behaviour.

questions.explanation: Dismissing an objective task proposal due to personal dislike shifts the conflict to a dysfunctional relationship level (A, C). The emotional personalization of their disagreement shapes defensive behavioral reactions, illustrating the Cognition and Personalisation stage (D).

questions.question_text: A company has two divisions: Sales and Production. Sales is rewarded based on order volume, while Production is rewarded for cost efficiency and waste minimisation. Conflict is constant. What are the structural causes here? (Select all that apply)

options.A: Goal incompatibility between the two units.
options.B: Jurisdictional ambiguities regarding who has final say over order speed.
options.C: Differences in "Personal Variables" like the personalities of the managers.
options.D: Interdependence, as one unit cannot succeed without the other.

questions.explanation: The conflict is driven by structural factors: Goal Incompatibility, as Sales targets raw volume while Production targets strict cost efficiency (A), and Task Interdependence, as Sales orders directly dictate and constrain Production operations (D).

questions.question_text: An organisation wants to implement a new AI-driven workflow. Using Lewin’s Force Field Analysis, how can they successfully move to the "desired state"? (Select all that apply)

options.A: Increase the driving forces (incentives for using AI).
options.B: Decrease the restraining forces (addressing fear of job loss).
options.C: Ignore the restraining forces to maintain momentum.
options.D: Combine increasing driving forces and decreasing restraining forces.

questions.explanation: According to Lewin's Force Field Analysis, changing status quo involves either amplifying the driving forces for change (A), diminishing the restraining forces/resistance against it (B), or executing a combination of both interventions (D).

questions.question_text: A sales manager is deciding how to evaluate her team. Which of the following are valid criteria for performance evaluation? (Select all that apply)

options.A: Individual task outcomes (total sales volume).
options.B: Behaviours (promptness in filing reports, teamwork).
options.C: Traits (having a "good attitude" or "being confident").
options.D: Citizenship behaviour (helping colleagues with their clients).

questions.explanation: Valid, objective performance metrics include output outcomes (sales volume), visible work behaviors (reporting speed), and organizational citizenship behaviors (helping peers). Assessing abstract traits (such as 'attitude' or 'confidence') is highly subjective and vulnerable to rater bias.

questions.question_text: To ensure that "Learning" actually translates into "Transfer" (using the skill on the job), an HR manager should: (Select all that apply)

options.A: Ensure the training environment matches the work environment.
options.B: Provide opportunities to practice the new skill immediately.
options.C: Use "Massed Practice" (one 8-hour session) instead of "Spaced Practice."
options.D: Support the trainee with a "culture of transfer" back at the office.

questions.explanation: Successful skill transfer requires physical and psychological similarity between the training and work setups (A), rapid post-training practice opportunities (B), and managerial support/reinforcement in the office environment (D).

questions.question_text: A startup decides to operate as a Virtual Organisation, outsourcing its manufacturing to China, its IT to India, and its marketing to a boutique firm in London. What are the primary advantages of this "Small Core" structure? (Select all that apply)

options.A: Maximum flexibility to adapt to market changes.
options.B: Significant savings by reducing permanent staff and physical overhead.
options.C: Total control over the day-to-day processes of all partners.
options.D: Clear and easy long-term career paths for all team members.

questions.explanation: The virtual ('small core') structure maximizes flexibility by letting organizations scale and pivot functions rapidly without committing resources (A), while keeping payroll and overhead expenses highly optimized (B).

questions.question_text: A CEO of a multinational firm sends a complex strategic directive regarding a merger to the regional VPs. The VPs summarise it for the Department Managers, who then translate it into specific tasks for their teams. By the time it reaches the front-line staff, the original intent regarding "cultural integration" has been replaced by "cost-cutting measures." Which of the following factors contributed to this outcome? (Select all that apply)

options.A: Information Filtering.
options.B: Message Distortion through the "Grapevine."
options.C: Channel Richness.
options.D: Selective Perception by middle management.

questions.explanation: This outcome is caused by Information Filtering (A), where hierarchical intermediaries deliberately refine or alter messages to fit expected goals, combined with Selective Perception (D), where middle managers interpret and project the directive based solely on their immediate, localized interests.

questions.question_text: During a high-stakes negotiation, the opposing side's lead negotiator says, "We are very interested in this partnership." Still, they are currently sitting with their arms tightly crossed, avoiding eye contact, and tapping their foot rapidly. What should a skilled observer conclude? (Select all that apply)

options.A: The verbal message is likely the only one that matters.
options.B: Non-verbal communication contradicts the verbal message.
options.C: The negotiator may be experiencing anxiety or discomfort.
options.D: The negotiator is definitely lying about their interest level.

questions.explanation: Body language, such as crossed arms, avoiding eye contact, and foot-tapping, represents defensive non-verbal cues that contradict the optimistic verbal assertion (B) and suggest the presence of stress, anxiety, or internal discomfort (C).

questions.question_text: A Project Manager receives 300 emails, 50 Slack messages, and 10 urgent "pings" on their phone every day. They have started missing important deadlines because they cannot distinguish between "urgent" and "important" tasks. What are the likely consequences of this scenario? (Select all that apply)

options.A: The manager will begin to "filter" information poorly.
options.B: Communication efficiency will increase due to the volume of data.
options.C: Vital information will be ignored or "lost" in the noise.
options.D: The manager will experience significant stress and burnout.

questions.explanation: Severe information overload limits cognitive capacity, leading to poor filtering of information (A), oversight of critical inputs lost within the sheer message volume (C), and physical or emotional burnout (D).

questions.question_text:
Analyse the context and answer the following question

You manage a department of five employees. You have identified that Joel has a high need for achievement, Gita has a high need for power, and Feroze has a high need for affiliation. Priya scored high on the need for power and low on the need for affiliation. Deep scored low on both need for power and need for affiliation.

Which of the following employees would likely thrive in an assignment characterised by high personal responsibility, moderate risks, and frequent performance feedback? (Select all that apply)

options.A: Joel
options.B: Gita
options.C: An employee who possesses a high nAch
options.D: Feroze

questions.explanation: According to McClelland's Theory of Needs, individuals with a high need for achievement (nAch) are motivated by personal accountability, moderately difficult challenges, and constant feedback on their performance. Both Joel (A) and anyone with a high nAch profile (C) fit this description.

questions.question_text:
Analyse the context and answer the following question

You manage a department of five employees. You have identified that Joel has a high need for achievement, Gita has a high need for power, and Feroze has a high need for affiliation. Priya scored high on the need for power and low on the need for affiliation. Deep scored low on both need for power and need for affiliation.

When selecting a temporary replacement to manage the department, which profiles typically align with the "Managerial Motive”? (Select all that apply)

options.A: Priya
options.B: Deep
options.C: Joel
options.D: Gita

questions.explanation: The 'Managerial Motive' is characterized by a high need for power (nPow) combined with a low need for affiliation (nAff). This allows leaders to exercise institutional influence and make tough, unbiased objective decisions. Priya and Gita possess this motivational blend.

questions.question_text: Which of the following factors would provide a strong argument against the immediate implementation of a job rotation program? (Select all that apply)

options.A: The organisation is entering its peak busy season with critical project deadlines.
options.B: A competitor recently reported higher employee engagement after rotating their staff.
options.C: The company's primary focus for the next month is to maximise immediate, short-term productivity.
options.D: Management has identified that the training and transition time for new roles will significantly disrupt current workflows.

questions.explanation: Job rotation requires learning and transition time, which temporarily degrades performance. Thus, entering peak periods (A), prioritizing short-term output (C), and anticipating severe workflow disruptions (D) are clear reasons not to implement it immediately.

questions.question_text:
The "Agile" Transformation of GlobalBank

GlobalBank, a century-old financial institution, is currently grappling with a pervasive "silo mentality" that hampers its operational efficiency. The lengthy decision-making processes, often spanning several months, are largely due to the need for extensive approvals from various departments, including the Risk Department, the Legal Department, and the Regional Vice President (VP). This cumbersome approval framework has stifled innovation and slowed the introduction of new products, particularly in the competitive landscape of financial technology.

In response to these challenges, the CEO is advocating a transformative shift to a boundaryless, team-based organisational structure. This approach aims to foster collaboration across departments, facilitating faster decision-making and enabling the bank to respond more quickly to market demands and better compete with agile fintech startups that thrive on speed and flexibility. By breaking down institutional barriers, GlobalBank hopes to cultivate a more dynamic environment that prioritises innovation and operational agility.

Which structural change is most likely to reduce the "horizontal boundaries" within GlobalBank?

options.A: Implementing a strict, unbroken Chain of Command.
options.B: Replacing functional departments with cross-functional "Tribes" focused on specific customer journeys.
options.C: Increasing the Span of Control for senior executives while maintaining current departments.
options.D: Centralising all IT and Risk decisions at the global headquarters.

questions.explanation: Horizontal boundaries run between different functional silos (like Risk, Legal, Sales). Creating cross-functional 'Tribes' colocates distinct experts to work collaboratively on unified customer journeys, effectively reducing these horizontal divisions.

questions.question_text:
[Refer to Question ID 37 for context]

If GlobalBank adopts a Team Structure, what is the primary behavioural risk management that must be mitigated to prevent a drop in performance?

options.A: Increased standard operating procedures (SOPs).
options.B: Loss of "Unity of Command" causing employee role conflict and stress.
options.C: Reduced need for interpersonal and conflict-resolution training.
options.D: Excessive vertical communication is slowing down the frontline.

questions.explanation: Sifting to cross-functional teams and matrix layouts dilutes traditional reporting, leading to a loss of 'Unity of Command'. Employees often receive instructions from multiple sources, causing stress and severe role conflict.

questions.question_text:
[Refer to Question ID 37 for context]

To support this new "Agile" structure, how should GlobalBank adjust its Formalisation?

options.A: Increase formalisation to ensure the new teams don't deviate from banking regulations.
options.B: Maintain high formalisation to protect the bank's legacy culture.
options.C: Decrease formalisation to allow teams to iterate, experiment, and pivot quickly.
options.D: Formalise only the communication channels, but not the actual work processes.

questions.explanation: Formalization represents standardization and rigidity. To support agility, teams need flexibility to iterate and experiment; thus, reducing formalization is necessary to prevent bureaucracy from slowing down innovation.

questions.question_text:
[Refer to Question ID 37 for context]

The CEO’s move toward a "Boundaryless" structure specifically targets the elimination of "Vertical Boundaries." Which action would most effectively achieve this?

options.A: Implementing a 360-degree performance appraisal system where subordinates evaluate their managers.
options.B: Adding two more layers of middle management to ensure the new "Tribes" are monitored.
options.C: Enforcing a strict "Scalar Chain" where every message must pass through the Regional VP.
options.D: Expanding the use of Job Specialisation to ensure every team member has a narrow, expert focus.

questions.explanation: Vertical boundaries represent the hierarchy separating rank levels. Introducing multi-directional, upward feedback like 360-degree performance appraisals bridges this social distance, promoting flat, vertical integration.

questions.question_text:
[Refer to Question ID 37 for context]

If GlobalBank’s environment is characterised by high "Volatility" (market shifts) and high "Complexity" (regulatory requirements), how does Robbins’ Contingency Theory suggest the structure should be balanced?

options.A: The organisation should be 100% Mechanistic to handle the complexity.
options.B: The organisation should be 100% Organic to handle the volatility.
options.C: The organisation should use an Organic structure for responsiveness but maintain specific "Mechanistic" pockets for regulatory compliance.
options.D: The organisation should revert to a Simple Structure to ensure the CEO has total control.

questions.explanation: Robbins' theory notes that when facing multiple environmental contingencies, structures must balance priorities. A hybrid approach of organic wings for market responsiveness, while keeping mechanistic clusters to enforce complex regulations, is the optimal compromise.

questions.question_text:
The Cultural Erosion at "BlueJet Airlines"

BlueJet, once renowned for its vibrant "Family First" culture, fostered an environment where employees thrived in casual attire, shared light-hearted jokes over the intercom, and enjoyed a high degree of empowerment in their roles. This welcoming atmosphere not only encouraged camaraderie among staff but also translated into exceptional customer service. However, the dynamics shifted dramatically with the appointment of a new CEO hailing from a traditional legacy carrier. This new leadership brought a stringent corporate ethos, marked by the enforcement of formal uniforms, rigidly timed bathroom breaks, and the introduction of a staggering 500-page manual detailing the protocol for every conceivable task.

The abrupt change alienated employees, many of whom felt their individuality and autonomy were being stifled. Within a mere year, the tension reached a boiling point as flight attendants, feeling undervalued and overregulated, resorted to striking. This rebellion against the new policies highlighted the discontent brewing within the workforce. Concurrently, customer satisfaction, which had previously flourished under the relaxed and engaging atmosphere, began to plummet, signalling a stark decline in the company’s once-cherished reputation for service excellence.

What occurred to BlueJet’s culture under the new CEO?

options.A: The culture became "stronger" due to more rules.
options.B: The CEO failed to act as a visible role model for the original culture.
options.C: The culture shifted from a high-trust to a high-formalisation environment.
options.D: The organisation experienced "Refreezing" too early.

questions.explanation: The introduction of formal uniforms, strict timing rules, and an extensive 500-page operational manual signifies a dramatic structural pivot away from informal high-trust empowerment toward an intensely bureaucratic, highly formalized environment.

questions.question_text:
[Refer to Question ID 43 for context]

The flight attendants' strike represents which source of resistance to change?

options.A: Individual: Habit.
options.B: Organisational: Structural Inertia.
options.C: Organisational: Threat to established power relationships.
options.D: Individual: Fear of the unknown.

questions.explanation: The sudden structural standardization directly undermined the high degree of employee empowerment, autonomy, and voice that flight attendants formerly enjoyed. This strike is an active resistance to defend those established relationships and power configurations.

questions.question_text:
[Refer to Question ID 43 for context]

Which step of Lewin’s model did the CEO likely skip?

options.A: Unfreezing.
options.B: Movement.
options.C: Refreezing.
options.D: Evaluation.

questions.explanation: By introducing sweeping new regulations and manual-driven tasks overnight without prepping the staff or showing the clear necessity of these changes, the CEO skipped 'Unfreezing'—the critical stage required to overcome existing status quo inertia.

questions.question_text:
[Refer to Question ID 43 for context]

To fix the strike, the CEO invites the union leader to sit on the board of directors, but gives them no real power. This is an example of:

options.A: Education.
options.B: Participation.
options.C: Co-optation.
options.D: Coercion.

questions.explanation: Co-optation is a structural form of manipulation that involves offering key resistance figures a symbolic role in the decision-making process to secure their endorsement, while withholding any genuine influence or authority.

questions.question_text:
[Refer to Question ID 43 for context]

How could the CEO have used "Socialisation" to make this change more effective?

options.A: By firing all old employees and hiring new ones.
options.B: By conducting orientation programs that explain the "why" behind the new professional standards.
options.C: By ignoring the old culture entirely.
options.D: By increasing the "Divestiture" socialisation to strip away old identities.

questions.explanation: Socialization is the process of integrating people into a culture or standard. Conducting orientation sessions that transparently unpack the rationale ('the why') behind the updated operational standards would have helped employees align with the change voluntarily.

questions.question_text:
The "Remote Work" Performance Appraisal

"CloudScale" operates as a fully remote company, leveraging a modern work culture that emphasises flexibility, autonomy, and trust. This innovative virtual environment empowers employees to manage their own schedules and work styles, as managers do not directly monitor their daily activities. This approach cultivates a sense of ownership among team members, allowing them to tailor their work processes to what they consider most effective for their individual productivity and creativity.

To accurately evaluate performance and contributions, CloudScale employs a Management by Objectives (MBO) framework. This method involves establishing clear, measurable goals collaboratively defined by managers and employees. By focusing on quantifiable outcomes and specific achievements rather than simply tracking activity levels, this performance appraisal system promotes a results-oriented culture. It ensures that evaluations are fair and based on actual contributions, aligning with the company’s commitment to optimising the effectiveness of remote work. This goal-oriented structure not only enhances transparency but also motivates employees to strive for excellence and take initiative in achieving their objectives.

In an MBO system, goals are set:

options.A: Solely by the manager.
options.B: Solely by the employee.
options.C: Jointly by the manager and employee.
options.D: By the HR department without consulting the manager.

questions.explanation: The defining hallmark of any functional Management by Objectives (MBO) system is that objectives are not unilaterally imposed; rather, they are established through active joint collaboration between the manager and employee.

questions.question_text:
[Refer to Question ID 49 for context]

For a remote company, evaluating "Behaviours" (like what time they log on) is often less effective than evaluating:

options.A: Traits (Personality).
options.B: Task Outcomes (Results produced).
options.C: Physical appearance.
options.D: Seniority.

questions.explanation: In a remote arrangement where employees manage their own schedules and direct physical monitoring is absent, traditional behavioral inputs (e.g., login times) are unreliable. Performance systems should instead evaluate concrete task outcomes and actual deliverables produced.

questions.question_text:
[Refer to Question ID 49 for context]

If a remote manager at CloudScale gives a high rating to an employee just because they respond to emails instantly (even if the work quality is poor), the manager is suffering from:

options.A: The "Availability" heuristic (evaluating based on visible info).
options.B: The "Contrast" error.
options.C: The "Similarity" error.
options.D: A central tendency error.

questions.explanation: The availability heuristic occurs when a rater relies heavily on the most visible, vivid, or easily accessible pieces of information (like instant email responses) to make a broad judgment, while ignoring less salient but more critical quality data.

questions.question_text:
[Refer to Question ID 49 for context]

CloudScale uses "Peer Appraisals" where developers rate each other's code. This is useful because:

options.A: Peers have a more intimate view of daily performance than remote managers.
options.B: Peers are always 100% objective and never biased.
options.C: It allows the manager to stop working entirely.
options.D: It reduces the amount of work for the employee.

questions.explanation: Because remote managers do not observe daily activities directly, peer appraisals are highly beneficial. Colleagues interact constantly on tasks and possess a direct, accurate understanding of each other's actual contributions and work quality.

questions.question_text:
[Refer to Question ID 49 for context]

To ensure the MBO system works, the goals must be:

options.A: Vague and flexible.
options.B: SMART (Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Results-oriented, and Time-bound).
options.C: Easy enough for everyone to achieve.
options.D: Set once every 10 years.

questions.explanation: Goal setting is functional only when objectives are formulated to be SMART—Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Results-oriented, and Time-bound—allowing for clear evaluation, accountability, and tracking.

questions.question_text:
The "Always-On" Culture at FinTech Corp

FinTech Corp is a rapidly growing startup that has garnered attention for its high-pressure work environment, largely driven by the CEO's unwavering work ethic and a pervasive "24/7 hustle" mentality. This philosophy often manifests as employees receiving Slack messages at all hours, including 2 AM, with the implicit expectation that they respond without delay.

To support this intense work culture, the company stocks its pantry with a variety of free energy drinks, ranging from caffeinated sodas to energy shots, intended to keep employees alert and productive. Additionally, the company has invested in ergonomically designed "nap pods" throughout the office, providing workers a designated space to recharge during the day. However, these amenities are accompanied by a relentless pressure, making it difficult for employees to take genuine breaks without feeling the weight of their workload.

Recently, the consequences of this high-octane culture became alarmingly apparent when three of the company’s top developers reported experiencing severe symptoms of stress, such as heart palpitations and debilitating anxiety. These health concerns ultimately led to their resignations, raising significant red flags about the sustainability of such a demanding work environment. The situation underscores the critical need to evaluate the impact of extreme work expectations on employee well-being and overall productivity, highlighting the potential long-term repercussions of prioritising relentless hustle over health and balance.

The heart palpitations suffered by the developers are categorised as:

options.A: Psychological symptoms.
options.B: Physiological symptoms.
options.C: Behavioural symptoms.
options.D: Environmental symptoms.

questions.explanation: Stress can affect individuals in three main areas: physiological, psychological, and behavioral. Heart palpitations represent a direct, physical somatic reaction of the body, classifying them as physiological symptoms.

questions.question_text:
[Refer to Question ID 55 for context]

The 2 AM messages create a stressor known as:

options.A: Inter-role conflict (work-life blurring).
options.B: Role ambiguity.
options.C: Challenge stressor.
options.D: Role underload.

questions.explanation: Receiving and being expected to reply to work communications in the middle of the night (2 AM) blurs the boundaries between professional duties and private personal time, resulting in inter-role conflict.

questions.question_text:
[Refer to Question ID 55 for context]

The "nap pods" and "energy drinks" are examples of:

options.A: Addressing the root cause of stress.
options.B: Individual stress management.
options.C: Organisational wellness programs that address symptoms, not stressors.
options.D: Goal setting.

questions.explanation: Amenities like nap pods and energy drinks are organizational coping mechanisms. They assist employees in managing fatigue (the symptoms of long hours) rather than addressing the structural work expectations and constant availability demands that cause the stress in the first place.

questions.question_text:
[Refer to Question ID 55 for context]

If a developer feels they must answer the 2 AM message to get a promotion, but also wants to sleep to be healthy, they are facing:

options.A: Inter-role conflict.
options.B: Person-role conflict.
options.C: Role overload.
options.D: Role underload.

questions.explanation: Person-role conflict arises when the behavioral requirements of an organizational role (responding at 2 AM) directly clash with an individual's personal needs, health values, or personal boundaries (needing sleep to stay healthy).

questions.question_text:
[Refer to Question ID 55 for context]

To structurally reduce this stress, the company should move toward:

options.A: Increasing formalisation.
options.B: Implementing "Right to Disconnect" policies (Organisational strategy).
options.C: Offering more energy drinks.
options.D: Hiring only people who don't sleep.

questions.explanation: To resolve the underlying issues, the company should establish organizational strategies like a formal 'Right to Disconnect' policy, protecting personal boundaries and defining clear timeframes when employees are not expected to check work communications.

questions.question_text:
The "Legacy Motors" Turnaround

Sarah has recently taken the helm as the CEO of a venerable automotive plant that boasts a rich history spanning over 70 years. The atmosphere within the facility is charged with a mix of scepticism and resistance, particularly among the workforce, which is unionised and entrenched in traditional practices. Many assembly line workers are seasoned artisans, with a wealth of experience and skill in their roles. However, they are at a disadvantage, lacking the technical training needed to transition to electric vehicles (EVs) and the intricate work involved in cutting-edge EV battery technology.

In this complex environment, mid-level managers, though competent in their duties, are often paralysed by the looming pressure of a high-stakes landscape. Their apprehension about making mistakes stifles innovation and progress, creating a tense and cautious atmosphere. Against this backdrop, Sarah enters with a limited budget for bonuses. Yet she carries a clear and inspiring vision for the plant's future-one that aims to navigate the challenges ahead and usher in a new era of sustainable manufacturing.

The assembly line workers are technically proficient in old methods but "unskilled and hesitant" regarding the new EV tech. How should Sarah approach them initially?

options.A: Empower them by delegating all transition decisions to their union reps.
options.B: Provide highly specific, step-by-step technical instructions and monitor the floor closely.
options.C: Focus purely on building emotional rapport and trust without mentioning technical specs.
options.D: Set high-performance targets and assume their prior skill will transfer naturally.

questions.explanation: Since the employees lack technical competence in EV battery assembly and feel apprehensive about the change, they fit a 'low competence, low confidence' readiness profile. Under situational leadership theory, this calls for highly specific, step-by-step guidance and close supervision.

questions.question_text:
[Refer to Question ID 61 for context]

The mid-level managers are "capable but apprehensive" about the new risk-heavy environment. What should Sarah emphasise to maximise their performance?

options.A: Increase the formal penalties for any operational errors.
options.B: Reduce her involvement entirely to show she trusts them.
options.C: Increase two-way communication and involve them in decision-making to build their confidence.
options.D: Use a "telling" style to ensure they don't deviate from her vision.

questions.explanation: For individuals who possess high capability but are hesitant or risk-averse, a participative style is ideal. Increasing two-way communication and involving them in decision-making builds confidence, reduces performance anxiety, and helps overcome their fear of errors.

questions.question_text:
[Refer to Question ID 61 for context]

Sarah decides to hold town halls where she questions long-held industry myths and asks workers to imagine "transportation" rather than just "cars." This behaviour is an example of:

options.A: Management by Exception.
options.B: Contingent Reward Systems.
options.C: Intellectual Stimulation.
options.D: Passive-avoidant leadership.

questions.explanation: Intellectual Stimulation is a key dimension of Transformational Leadership. It involves encouraging followers to challenge long-standing assumptions, rethink established operational conventions, and view industry problems from entirely new angles.

questions.question_text:
[Refer to Question ID 61 for context]

Despite Sarah’s hard work, the plant’s stock price rises primarily because a competitor went bankrupt. However, the Board of Directors publicly credits Sarah’s "divine insight" for the success. This illustrates:

options.A: The Substitutes for Leadership model.
options.B: The Attribution Theory of Leadership.
options.C: Socialised Power.
options.D: Individualised Consideration.

questions.explanation: The Attribution Theory of Leadership posits that leadership is a label or perception that observers attribute to individuals. In this case, the Board attributes the rise in stock price to Sarah's leadership qualities rather than recognizing the external cause (the competitor's bankruptcy).

questions.question_text:
[Refer to Question ID 61 for context]

To ensure long-term stability, Sarah begins training "Successor Leaders" who share her values but are encouraged to develop their own styles. This indicates she is focused on:

options.A: Personalised Charisma.
options.B: Self-Serving Influence.
options.C: Stewardship and Servant-based behaviour.
options.D: Coercive Power.

questions.explanation: Fostering organizational sustainability, investing in succession planning, and helping other leaders grow while allowing them autonomy are key behaviors of stewardship and servant leadership, prioritizing the organization's legacy over personal control.

questions.question_text:
The "Digital Transformation" Deadlock

Global Logistics Inc. is in the midst of a significant digital transformation, shifting to an AI-driven routing system to optimise delivery efficiency and reduce operational costs. The Operations Team, whose performance is evaluated on speed and cost-effectiveness, is eager to implement the new software immediately to meet demanding quarterly targets and boost profitability. They believe that advanced routing algorithms will significantly streamline operations and enhance customer satisfaction by reducing delivery times.

On the other hand, the IT Security Team, which prioritises risk mitigation and system integrity, is apprehensive about the launch. They have identified several minor vulnerabilities within the software that could potentially expose the company to security threats. Addressing these issues would require months of thorough assessment and patching to ensure that the system can be deployed without jeopardising sensitive company and client data.

The situation has deteriorated to the point that communication between the two department heads has completely broken down. This discord has not only stymied progress on the project but has also started to impact the broader company culture. Employees across various teams have expressed concerns about rising tension, which has led to a noticeable decline in overall morale and collaboration within the organisation. The CEO has observed this shift and is under pressure to intervene and find a resolution before it further affects productivity and staff retention.

The conflict over the "launch date" vs. "security patches" is primarily categorised as:

options.A: Relationship Conflict.
options.B: Task Conflict.
options.C: Process Conflict.
options.D: Dyadic Conflict.

questions.explanation: The disagreement between the two departments focuses strictly on the work goals and content of their project (whether to prioritize speed/launch or security patching). This content-driven friction is classified as task conflict.

questions.question_text:
[Refer to Question ID 67 for context]

The fact that Operations is rewarded for speed while IT is rewarded for safety represents which "Structural Variable" of conflict?

options.A: Jurisdictional Ambiguity.
options.B: Goal Incompatibility.
options.C: Personal Variable.
options.D: Communication Barrier.

questions.explanation: Goal incompatibility is a structural variable of organizational conflict. It occurs when two units are given distinct performance standards and incentive structures that push them in opposite directions (e.g., speed of release vs. complete safety).

questions.question_text:
[Refer to Question ID 67 for context]

The department heads' refusal to speak to each other signifies that the conflict has moved into which stage?

options.A: Cognition and Personalisation.
options.B: Intentions.
options.C: Behaviour.
options.D: Potential Opposition.

questions.explanation: Refusing to speak with each other is an active, visible action. This means the conflict has progressed past internal cognition or intentions into Stage IV: Behaviour, where frustration is expressed through overt conduct.

questions.question_text:
[Refer to Question ID 67 for context]

If the CEO forces the teams to find a solution that satisfies both the speed requirements and the security protocols without compromise, she is encouraging:

options.A: Compromising.
options.B: Accommodating.
options.C: Collaborating.
options.D: Competing.

questions.explanation: Collaborating is a win-win conflict resolution style where both parties work to find an integration that fully meets the essential goals of both sides (operational speed AND security safety) without requiring either to compromise on key concerns.

questions.question_text:
[Refer to Question ID 67 for context]

Research suggests that the "Task Conflict" in this case would only be functional (beneficial) if:

options.A: The levels of Relationship Conflict remain very low.
options.B: The CEO makes the final decision unilaterally.
options.C: The IT Security team eventually gives in to Operations.
options.D: The conflict is ignored until the next quarter.

questions.explanation: Task conflict is beneficial because it brings diverse ideas and prevents groupthink. However, research proves that task conflict only remains functional if relationship conflict (personal clashes and emotional animosity) is kept at very low levels.
